findings.title: Assert failure leaves partition stuck forever
findings.body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the assert `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is performed before accessing `message.value`. If it fails (or any other error occurs before we can safely read `message.value`), the `except Exception` handler re-checks `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` — which is the same condition that just failed — and silently does nothing. The offset for that message is never added to the tracker, so it stays outstanding and blocks every future commit for that partition in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (which iterates only up to the highest completed offset). The consumer will hang on this partition indefinitely, with only a log line as evidence. The error should either be re-raised so arroyo/DLQ can handle it, or the offset must be marked complete unconditionally (even if `BrokerValue` can't be read) by carrying the partition/offset before the assert.

findings.title: Graceful shutdown drops in-flight queue items
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `self.work_queue.get()`, workers exit the loop as soon as the flag is observed and never drain items that were already in their queue. Those items have offsets recorded as outstanding in `OffsetTracker`, but since `complete_offset` is never called, they will never be committed and the messages will be re-delivered after restart. The `wait_until_empty` helper exists on the same class but is never invoked, indicating the intent was to drain but the implementation doesn't. Either remove the `wait_until_empty` helper or call it (with a bounded timeout) before flipping the shutdown flag.

findings.title: Hash-based group assignment is not stable across restarts
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which is randomized per process under the default `PYTHONHASHSEED`. The class docstring promises 'consistent hashing' and 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue'. Within a single process lifetime the assignment is stable (since workers/queues live in memory), but after any restart the same `group_key` can map to a different queue index — directly contradicting the docstring. This is misleading to future maintainers and would break correctness if the pool is ever extended to persist queue assignments or run across processes. Use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.sha1(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()`, `zlib.crc32`, or `hashlib.md5`) and update the docstring to reflect the actual guarantee.

findings.title: Docstring claims natural backpressure but queue is unbounded
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. However, the queues are constructed via `queue.Queue()` (see `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), which is unbounded. Producers (the arroyo consumer thread calling `submit`) will never block, so a slow worker group causes unbounded memory growth. Either pass `maxsize` to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to actually provide backpressure, or correct the docstring.

findings.title: Worker shutdown flag is a non-atomic bool
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a plain `bool` attribute written by the main thread (in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`) and read by the worker thread. While CPython's GIL makes this safe in practice, it is not portable and is not thread-safe by Python's memory model. Use `threading.Event` (`self._stop_event`) and `self._stop_event.is_set()` instead, matching the pattern already used by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.shutdown_event`.

findings.title: num_queues is not validated
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` accepts `num_queues: int = 20` without checking it is positive. If a caller (or the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode) passes `max_workers=0` or a negative value, the loop creates no queues/workers, and the first call to `submit` raises `IndexError` from `self.queues[queue_index]` deep in `FixedQueuePool.submit`. Validate `num_queues >= 1` (and ideally a sensible upper bound) at construction time so misconfiguration fails loudly and early.

findings.title: Offset tracker scans full range per partition every second
findings.body: `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` is called once per second from `_commit_loop` and, for each partition, computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` and then iterates the full range `range(start, max_offset + 1)`. With a partition that has, say, 10k outstanding offsets, every commit tick performs O(10k) set lookups plus two O(n) set scans. For a backlog scenario this is O(n) per second per partition. Track `min_offset` and `max_offset` incrementally (e.g. on `add_offset`) and stop as soon as the first gap is hit instead of recomputing the extremes every call.

findings.title: Worker thread can die silently on unexpected get() error
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` only catches `queue.ShutDown` around `self.work_queue.get()`. Any other exception raised by `get()` (e.g. an OS-level error, a future Python version change) propagates out of `run()` and kills the daemon thread silently — items remaining in that queue will never be processed and their offsets will never be marked complete, permanently blocking that partition's commits. Wrap the call in a broader `except Exception` that logs and either retries or exits cleanly, and consider asserting the worker is still alive from a supervisor.

findings.title: Integration test relies on arroyo private internals
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. The leading underscore marks these as private arroyo APIs; their names/signatures are not part of arroyo's public contract and can change without warning, breaking this test (and the CI signal it provides) on an arroyo upgrade. Use the public `StreamProcessor.run()` method (which blocks until the consumer stops) instead, with a bounded stop condition or shutdown timeout, so the test exercises the same path real deployments use.

findings.title: Kafka integration test only waits 5 seconds for 5 messages
findings.body: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit`, the test produces 5 messages and then runs `processor._run_once()` in a loop for only 5 seconds. The assertions then require that `commit_count >= 1` and that the committed offset reached 5, but the producer flush + consumer rebalance + first poll can easily eat most of that budget on a loaded CI box, producing a flaky test. Wait for `stats["total_items"] == 0` (as the other tests in this file do) before tearing the processor down, and assert on the committed offset only after that condition is met.

findings.title: max_workers silently coerced to 20 when zero/falsy
findings.body: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` falls back to 20 whenever `max_workers` is `None`, `0`, or any other falsy value. An operator who passes `--max-workers 0` to disable the new mode will instead get 20 queues/workers started, with no log or error. The fallback should be explicit (`max_workers if max_workers else 20` is functionally the same but at minimum document the behavior, or raise on non-positive values so operators notice the misconfiguration).
